mainTopic: אלכסנדרוס מוקדון questions the זקני הנגב about creation, wisdom and life, then sets out for אפריקי.
overview: This amud continues the story of אלכסנדרוס מוקדון questioning the זקני הנגב. First he asks whether the sky is higher than the world is wide. The elders say east to west is farther. חכמים say the two distances are equal, based on a פסוק in תהלים. Next he asks about the order of creation. The elders answer that the heavens came first, but they refuse to say whether light or darkness came first, so that he will not go on to ask about forbidden topics. He then asks who is truly wise, mighty and rich, how to live, and how to win people's favor. On that last question he offers his own answer. After a tense exchange in which he threatens the elders, he honors them instead. Finally they advise him how to cross the Mountains of Darkness. He reaches a town of women, who talk him out of fighting and serve him bread of gold. The story continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Which distance is greater?
steps.stepSummary: אלכסנדרוס מוקדון asks whether the distance from heaven to earth is greater than the distance from east to west.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is it farther from the heavens to the earth, or from east to west?
steps.whatsHappening: The king asks the elders a question about the size of the world. This question sets up the debate that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He is comparing two huge distances: the height of the sky and the width of the world. The rest of this section argues over which one is bigger.

phrases.english: Is it farther from the heavens to the earth,
or from east to west?

steps.triggerLanguage: מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם לָאָרֶץ רָחוֹק, אוֹ מִמִּזְרָח לַמַּעֲרָב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next question in the king's series of questions to the elders.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which distance is greater: heaven to earth, or east to west.

steps.title: East to west is farther, proven from the sun
steps.stepSummary: The elders answer that east to west is farther. They prove it from the fact that people can look at the sun when it rises and sets, but not when it is overhead.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: from east to west. Know that this is true, because when the sun is in the east, everyone can look at it. When the sun is in the west, everyone can look at it. But when the sun is in the middle of the sky, no one can look at it.
steps.whatsHappening: The elders give their answer and back it up with an everyday observation about the sun.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their logic is that a closer sun is brighter and harder to look at. Since the overhead sun hurts the eyes, it must be closer to us than the sun at the far east or far west edges. So the height of the sky is less than the width of the world.

keyTerms.meaning: know (that this is so), introducing a proof

phrases.english: They said to him: from east to west.
Know that this is so, for when the sun is in the east,
everyone looks at it,
phrases.notes: They mean everyone can look at it without it hurting their eyes.

phrases.english: when the sun is in the west, everyone looks at it,
when the sun is in the middle of the sky,
no one looks at it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 1.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: East to west is the greater distance, as shown by how hard it is to look at the overhead sun.

steps.title: חכמים say both distances are equal
steps.stepSummary: חכמים disagree with the elders and say both distances are the same, based on פסוקים in תהלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: But חכמים say: both distances are equal, as it says: 'As high as the heavens are above the earth... as far as the east is from the west.'
steps.whatsHappening: A second opinion is brought. חכמים hold that the two distances are exactly equal, and they bring a פסוק as their source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוקים in תהלים use the two distances side by side as pictures: the height of the sky for how great ה׳'s kindness is, and east to west for how far He removes our sins. חכמים understand from this that the two distances are equal. The next step explains exactly how the פסוק proves this.

phrases.english: But the sages say:
this and that are equally the same,
as it is said: 'As the heavens are high above the earth [etc.]
phrases.notes: תהלים 103:11–12. וְגוֹ׳ means 'and so on': the פסוק keeps going past what's quoted.

phrases.english: as far as the east is from the west.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים: זֶה וָזֶה כְּאֶחָד שָׁוִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the elders' answer in step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The distance from heaven to earth equals the distance from east to west.

steps.title: How the verse proves they are equal
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the proof: if one distance were bigger, the פסוק would have used the bigger one for both comparisons.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if one of them were bigger, the פסוק should have written both comparisons using the bigger one!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how חכמים learn from the פסוק that the distances are equal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק wants to describe ה׳'s kindness and forgiveness as being as great as possible. If one distance were larger, it would have used that larger distance for both. Since it uses each distance once, the two must be the same size.

phrases.english: And if one of them were greater,
let it write both like the one that is greater!
phrases.notes: 'Both' means both things the פסוק praises: ה׳'s kindness and how far He removes our sins.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the proof from the פסוק in step 3.
steps.raayaObject: That the two distances are equal.
steps.raayaSupportSource: תהלים 103:11–12, which uses each distance once for comparison.

steps.title: Then why can't we look at the overhead sun?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: according to חכמים, how do we explain the elders' observation that the overhead sun is too bright to look at?
steps.simpleTranslation: But then, when the sun is in the middle of the sky, what is the reason no one can look at it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges חכמים with the elders' proof. If the overhead sun is not closer, why is it harder to look at?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The elders' proof from step 2 still needs an answer. If both distances are equal, closeness cannot be the reason the overhead sun hurts the eyes, so some other reason is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: but if so, then (introducing a difficulty)

phrases.english: But if so, the sun in the middle of the sky,

phrases.aramaic: מַאי טַעְמָא אֵין הַכֹּל מִסְתַּכְּלִין בָּהּ –
phrases.english: what is the reason no one looks at it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֶלָּא, חַמָּה בְּאֶמְצַע רָקִיעַ מַאי טַעְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the elders' proof from step 2 against the view of חכמים in steps 3–4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The opinion of חכמים that the distances are equal.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The overhead sun is harder to look at, which suggests it is closer.

steps.title: The overhead sun is uncovered
steps.stepSummary: The overhead sun is hard to look at because nothing blocks it, not because it is closer.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because it stands out in the open, and nothing covers it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the overhead sun is fully exposed, so its brightness is not blocked by anything.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the sun is low in the east or west, something partly screens it, so it is easier to look at. At midday nothing covers it. So the difference in brightness is about covering, not distance, and the view of חכמים stands.
steps.whatToRemember: The elders say east to west is farther because of the sun. חכמים say the distances are equal, based on the פסוק in תהלים, and explain the bright midday sun as simply uncovered.

phrases.english: Because it stands in the open,
and nothing covers it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives a different reason for the observation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The overhead sun is harder to look at because it is closer.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is harder to look at only because it is fully exposed.

steps.title: Heaven or earth: which was created first?
steps.stepSummary: The king asks whether the heavens or the earth was created first.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: were the heavens created first, or the earth?
steps.whatsHappening: The king moves on to a new question, this time about the order of creation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This starts a new topic. The question is no longer about size but about which part of the world came into being first.

phrases.english: He said to them:
Were the heavens created first, or the earth?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶן: שָׁמַיִם נִבְרְאוּ תְּחִלָּה אוֹ הָאָרֶץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new question in the king's series.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether heaven or earth was created first.

steps.title: The heavens came first
steps.stepSummary: The elders answer that the heavens came first, because the פסוק mentions them first.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: the heavens were created first, as it says: 'In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.'
steps.whatsHappening: The elders answer and prove it from the very first פסוק of the תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their proof is from the order of the words. Since the פסוק names the heavens before the earth, they understand that the heavens were created first.

phrases.english: They said: the heavens were created first,
as it is said: 'In the beginning God created
the heavens and the earth.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The heavens were created first, since the פסוק lists them first.

steps.title: Light or darkness: which was created first?
steps.stepSummary: The king asks whether light or darkness was created first.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: was light created first, or darkness?
steps.whatsHappening: The king asks another question about the order of creation, this time about light and darkness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This question has the same form as the last one. The elders' surprising answer in the next step will lead to a challenge from the גמרא.

phrases.english: He said to them:
Was light created first, or darkness?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶן: אוֹר נִבְרָא תְּחִלָּה, אוֹ חֹשֶׁךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another new question in the king's series.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether light or darkness was created first.

steps.title: The elders say there is no answer
steps.stepSummary: The elders reply that this question cannot be solved.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: this matter has no solution.
steps.whatsHappening: The elders refuse to give a definite answer and say the question has no solution.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the last question, here they do not bring a פסוק. This sets up the גמרא's challenge in the next step.

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: מִילְּתָא דָּא אֵין לַהּ פָּתַר.
phrases.english: They said to him: this matter has no solution.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: מִילְּתָא דָּא אֵין לַהּ פָּתַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the question of step 9.

steps.title: Why not say darkness came first?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the elders did not answer that darkness came first, since the פסוקים mention darkness before light.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let them say to him that darkness was created first, as it is written: 'And the earth was empty and void, and darkness,' and only afterward: 'And God said: Let there be light, and there was light'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the elders' answer. It points out that the פסוקים seem to clearly show darkness came before light. The next step answers this challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The elders used the order of the words in the last question, so the same method should work here. Darkness is mentioned in פסוק 2, and light is created only in פסוק 3. So why did they say there is no answer?
steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume the elders were wrong. The next step explains why they chose not to answer.

phrases.english: But let them say to him that darkness was created first,
as it is written: 'And the earth was empty and void, and darkness,'

phrases.aramaic: וַהֲדַר ״וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים יְהִי אוֹר וַיְהִי אוֹר״!
phrases.english: and afterward: 'And God said: Let there be light, and there was light'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the elders' answer in step 10, using the same method they used in step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The elders' claim that the question has no solution.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The order of the פסוקים shows darkness was mentioned before light was created.

steps.title: The elders feared forbidden follow-up questions
steps.stepSummary: The elders did not answer about darkness and light because they worried the king would go on to ask about what is above, below, before and after the world.
steps.simpleTranslation: They thought: maybe he will come to ask what is above and what is below, what was before and what will be after.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 11. The elders could have answered, but they chose not to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer "it cannot be solved" was not about lacking knowledge. It was a deliberate choice. Talking about what came before light might open the door to questions about what existed before Creation, and those topics are not meant to be explored.

keyTerms.meaning: Before and after (here: before Creation and after the end of the world)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the elders' 'no answer' was a careful, protective choice and not a gap in their wisdom.

phrases.english: They thought: perhaps he will come to ask
what is above and what is below,
what is before and what is after.
phrases.notes: Literally 'in front and behind.' Here it means what came before Creation and what comes after the world ends.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 11
steps.terutzResolutionType: Hidden reason: the elders deliberately chose not to answer
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The elders should have said darkness came first, as the פסוקים show
steps.terutzMaskana: They knew the answer but kept quiet to avoid forbidden follow-up questions

steps.title: Then why did they answer about heaven?
steps.stepSummary: If the elders were worried about forbidden questions, they should not have answered the question about heaven and earth either.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, they should not have told him about heaven either!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer it just gave. The first question, about heaven and earth, was also about Creation, and the elders did answer that one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry about forbidden questions should apply equally to both questions. So why did the elders treat them differently?

phrases.english: If so,
they should not have told him about heaven either!
phrases.notes: This points back to step 8, where the elders said heaven was created first.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, שָׁמַיִם נָמֵי לָא נֵימְרוּ לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the תירוץ of step 12
steps.kashyaTarget: The explanation that the elders feared forbidden questions
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Inconsistency: the same fear should have stopped them from answering about heaven and earth

steps.title: A single question seemed harmless; a repeat question was a warning sign
steps.stepSummary: At first the elders thought the king's question was a one-time curiosity. When he asked again about Creation, they realized he might keep going, so they stopped answering.
steps.simpleTranslation: At first they thought he was asking only by chance. Once they saw that he asked again, they decided not to answer, so that he would not come to ask what is above, below, before and after.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the difference between the two questions. The first question looked like a passing curiosity. The second one showed a pattern.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing changed about the topic. What changed was what the elders could tell about the king's intent. A repeated line of questioning suggested he would dig deeper into forbidden areas, so they stopped there.
steps.whatToRemember: The elders answered the first Creation question but refused the second. Asking again showed the king might push into forbidden topics.

phrases.english: At first they thought
that he was merely asking by chance,
once they saw that he asked again,
they thought: let us not tell him,
perhaps he will come to ask
what is above, what is below,
what is before and what is after.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵעִיקָּרָא סְבוּר אַקְרַאי בְּעָלְמָא הוּא דְּקָא שָׁיֵיל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the קשיא of step 13
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction between a first question and a repeated one
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both Creation questions should be treated the same
steps.terutzMaskana: A single question looked harmless; repeating it signaled a risk of forbidden inquiry

steps.title: Who is called wise?
steps.stepSummary: The king asks the elders who deserves to be called wise.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Who is called wise?
steps.whatsHappening: The story moves on to a new set of questions. These are about how a person should live, not about Creation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This opens a series of three parallel questions: wise, mighty and rich. Each one asks what the title really means.

phrases.english: He said to them: Who is called wise?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic in the dialogue
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The true definition of a wise person

steps.title: The wise person sees what is coming
steps.stepSummary: The elders answer that a wise person is one who foresees the results of his actions.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Who is wise? One who sees what will come about.
steps.whatsHappening: The elders define wisdom as thinking ahead, not as knowing a lot of facts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wisdom here means being able to see the results of a choice before making it. It is a practical skill, not just knowledge.

phrases.english: They said to him: Who is wise?
One who sees what will be born.
phrases.notes: 'What will be born' means the outcome. A wise person sees where his actions will lead.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 15
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A wise person foresees the consequences of his actions

steps.title: Who is called mighty?
steps.stepSummary: The king asks who deserves to be called mighty.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Who is called mighty?
steps.whatsHappening: The king asks the second question in the series.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It has the same structure as the question about wisdom. Now he asks what true strength is.

phrases.english: He said to them: Who is called mighty?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next question in the series
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The true definition of a mighty person

steps.title: The mighty person controls his desires
steps.stepSummary: The elders answer that a mighty person is one who conquers his own desire.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Who is mighty? One who conquers his desire.
steps.whatsHappening: The elders say that real strength is inner self-control, not physical power.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer turns the idea of strength inward. Beating yourself is a greater victory than beating others.

keyTerms.meaning: His desire (his inner drive to do wrong)

phrases.english: They said to him: Who is mighty?
One who conquers his desire.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 17
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A mighty person masters his desire

steps.title: Who is called rich?
steps.stepSummary: The king asks who deserves to be called rich.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Who is called rich?
steps.whatsHappening: The king asks the third question in the series.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Again he asks for the real meaning of a common title, this time wealth.

phrases.english: He said to them: Who is called rich?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next question in the series
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The true definition of a rich person

steps.title: The rich person is happy with what he has
steps.stepSummary: The elders answer that a rich person is one who is happy with his portion.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Who is rich? One who is happy with his portion.
steps.whatsHappening: The elders define wealth as being content, not as owning a lot.
steps.deeperAnalysis: All three answers follow the same pattern. Each title (wise, mighty, rich) is redefined as an inner quality instead of an outward one.
steps.whatToRemember: Wise means seeing what is coming. Mighty means controlling yourself. Rich means being happy with what you have. Each one is an inner quality.

phrases.english: They said to him: Who is rich?
One who is happy with his portion.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 19
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A rich person is content with his portion

steps.title: What should a person do to live?
steps.stepSummary: The king asks what a person should do in order to live.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: What should a person do and live?
steps.whatsHappening: The king begins a new pair of questions, about living and dying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He is asking for the secret to a good, lasting life.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהֹן: מָה יַעֲבֵיד אִינִישׁ וְיִחְיֶה?
phrases.english: He said to them: What should a person do and live?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהֹן: מָה יַעֲבֵיד אִינִישׁ וְיִחְיֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new pair of questions
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How a person can ensure he lives

steps.title: To live, a person must 'kill himself'
steps.stepSummary: The elders answer with a paradox: to live, a person should 'kill himself', meaning he should live modestly and hold himself back.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: He should kill himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The elders answer with a surprising saying that is not meant literally.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person who holds back from luxuries and indulgence actually gains a longer, truer life.

keyTerms.meaning: He should 'kill himself' (holding back, living modestly)

steps.confusionAlert: This is NOT literal! 'Kill himself' is a figure of speech for living modestly and holding back from indulgence.

phrases.english: They said to him: He should kill himself.
phrases.notes: Not literally! The idea is to hold himself back and live simply.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 21
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Live modestly and hold back from indulgence

steps.title: What should a person do to die?
steps.stepSummary: The king asks the opposite question: what would cause a person to die?
steps.simpleTranslation: What should a person do and die?
steps.whatsHappening: The king asks the reverse of his last question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the גמרא does not repeat 'he said to them'. The question follows straight on from the previous answer.

phrases.english: What should a person do and die?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reverse of step 21
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What leads a person to death

steps.title: Spoiling oneself leads to death
steps.stepSummary: The elders answer that a person who indulges himself, 'keeping himself alive' with luxuries, brings on his own death.
steps.simpleTranslation: He should keep himself alive.
steps.whatsHappening: The elders give the mirror image of their previous answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Pampering oneself feels like living fully, but it actually wears a person down. This completes the paradox from step 22.

phrases.english: He should keep himself alive.
phrases.notes: He means pampering himself with every pleasure, which is what really harms a person.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 23
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: An indulgent life leads to death

steps.title: How can a person be liked by people?
steps.stepSummary: The king asks what a person should do to be accepted and liked by others.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: What should a person do to be accepted by people?
steps.whatsHappening: The king asks a new question about popularity and how to win people's favor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This question sets up the only place in the dialogue where the king disagrees with the elders.

keyTerms.meaning: And he will be accepted / liked

phrases.english: He said to them: What should a person do
and be accepted by people?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהֹן: מָה יַעֲבֵיד אִינִישׁ וְיִתְקַבֵּל עַל בְּרִיָּיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New question

steps.title: The elders: stay away from rulers
steps.stepSummary: The elders answer that a person should hate the king and the authorities, meaning he should keep away from those in power.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: He should hate the kingdom and the government.
steps.whatsHappening: The elders advise keeping a distance from those in power in order to be liked by ordinary people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People often dislike those who are close to rulers. Staying away from power keeps a person trusted and loved. The elders give this bold answer to the king himself.

keyTerms.meaning: The kingdom and the government (those in power)

phrases.english: They said: He should hate the kingdom and the government.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 25
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Keep away from the king and those in power

steps.title: The king offers a better answer
steps.stepSummary: The king rejects the elders' answer. He says a person should love the king and the authorities, and use that closeness to do good for people.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: My answer is better than yours. He should love the kingdom and the government, and do good for people.
steps.whatsHappening: For the first time, the king disagrees with the elders and offers his own answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The elders said to avoid power. The king says to use power: be close to the authorities, and use that connection to help others. That is what makes people love you.
steps.whatToRemember: The elders said to stay away from power to be liked. The king said to stay close to power and use it to help people.

phrases.english: He said to them: Mine is better than yours,
he should love the kingdom and the government,
and do good with people.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the answer of step 26
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The elders' advice to hate those in power
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Closeness to power can be used to benefit people, which wins their favor

steps.title: Better to live at sea or on land?
steps.stepSummary: The king asks whether a person is better off living at sea or on dry land.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Is it better to live at sea, or is it better to live on dry land?
steps.whatsHappening: The king asks another question in his series: where is the better place for a person to live, on the sea or on land?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a new topic in the king's list of questions. He gives two choices and wants the חכמים to pick one.

phrases.english: He said to them:
Is it better to live at sea,
or is it better to live on dry land?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new question in the king's series, after the exchange about the authorities.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which place is better for human life, sea or land?

steps.title: Dry land is better, since sailors are never at ease
steps.stepSummary: The elders say land is better, because people at sea have no peace of mind until they reach land.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: It is better to live on dry land, because everyone who goes down to the sea has no settled mind until they come up onto dry land.
steps.whatsHappening: The elders answer that dry land is better. They prove it from sailors, who stay anxious until they reach the shore.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They answer from experience, not just opinion. Even people who live at sea feel calm only when they reach land, so land must be the natural, better home.

keyTerms.meaning: Seafarers, literally those who go down to the sea
Their mind is settled / at ease

phrases.english: They said to him:
It is better to live on dry land,
since all who go down to the sea,
their minds are not settled
until they come up onto dry land.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 28.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Land is better, as shown by sailors who are uneasy until they reach land.

steps.title: Which of you is the wisest?
steps.stepSummary: The king asks which of the elders is wiser than the rest.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Which of you is the wisest?
steps.whatsHappening: The king stops asking about the world and asks about the elders themselves. He wants to know which one of them is the smartest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the questions were about general wisdom. Now the king wants to rank the חכמים against each other.

phrases.english: He said to them:
Which of you is wiser than the others?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶן: אֵידֵין מִנְּכוֹן חַכִּים יַתִּיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New question, turning from the world to the elders themselves.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Who among the elders is the wisest?

steps.title: We are all equal, because we answer as one
steps.stepSummary: The elders say they are all equally wise, since they gave every answer together.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: We are all equal, because every matter you asked us, we answered you as one.
steps.whatsHappening: The elders say none of them is wiser than the others. Their proof is that they gave every answer together, all agreeing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their proof comes from what the king just saw. All their answers came out with one voice, so no one stood out above the others.

phrases.english: They said to him:
We are all equal as one,
since every matter that you said to us,
we solved for you as one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 30.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: All are equally wise, as shown by their unanimous answers.

steps.title: Why do you stand against me?
steps.stepSummary: The king challenges the elders: why do the Jews oppose him?
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Why do you oppose me?
steps.whatsHappening: The king turns sharper and challenges the elders. He asks why they, the Jewish people, stand against him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not a request for information but an attack. The king is saying: I rule over you and my people are the majority, so why don't you go along with my ways?

phrases.english: He said to them:
What is this, that you oppose me!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶן: מָה דֵין אַתְרֵיסְתּוּן לְקִבְלִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from testing wisdom to confronting the elders.
steps.kashyaTarget: The Jewish people's refusal to accept the king's way of life.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Subjects who are the minority should give in to the ruler and the majority.

steps.title: Even the שטן sometimes wins
steps.stepSummary: The elders answer that being stronger does not make you right, since even the שטן sometimes wins.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: The שטן wins.
steps.whatsHappening: The elders answer in two short words. Winning or having power does not prove you are right, because sometimes even the שטן wins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The king's challenge assumed that power and numbers prove who is right. The elders reject that idea: the שטן often wins over people, yet he is wrong.

phrases.english: They said to him:
The Satan wins.
phrases.notes: In other words: winning does not mean you are right. Sometimes the wrong side wins.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the king's challenge in step 32.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Power and majority prove that the king's way is right.
steps.terutzMaskana: Winning proves nothing, since even the שטן wins at times.

steps.title: The king threatens to execute them
steps.stepSummary: Angered by their reply, the king threatens to kill them by royal decree.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Then I will kill you by royal decree!
steps.whatsHappening: The king is insulted by the comparison to the שטן. He threatens to have the elders put to death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The king answers their argument with force instead of logic. He is saying: you may call my power meaningless, but I can use it on you.

keyTerms.meaning: A royal decree, an order of kings

phrases.english: He said to them:
Now I am going to kill you
by the decree of kings!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהֹן: הָא אֲנָא מְקַטֵּילְנָא יָתְכוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reacts angrily to the answer in step 33.
steps.kashyaTarget: The elders' boldness in comparing the king's success to the שטן.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A threat of force: the king can still punish them.

steps.title: You have the power, but a king must not lie
steps.stepSummary: The elders agree that the king has the power, but say a king should not break his word.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: The power is in the king's hand, but lying is not fitting for a king.
steps.whatsHappening: The elders do not deny that the king can kill them. They remind him that lying, breaking his word, does not suit a king.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They admit the king's power and then point to his honor. If he kills them, he goes back on his word, and a king who lies loses his dignity.

phrases.english: They said to him:
Authority is in the hand of the king,
but falsehood is not fitting for a king.
phrases.notes: They mean: you promised earlier not to harm us, so killing us would make you a liar.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the threat in step 34.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Concedes the power but appeals to the king's honor
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the king has the power, he may simply kill them.
steps.terutzMaskana: Power alone is not enough. A king must keep his word.

steps.title: The king honors them with purple robes and gold chains
steps.stepSummary: The king accepts their answer and right away honors the elders with royal clothing and golden chains.
steps.simpleTranslation: Immediately he dressed them in purple garments and placed golden chains on their necks.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends this tense exchange. Instead of killing the elders, the king honors them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The threat turns into honor. The elders' wise answer won the king over, and purple clothing and gold chains were royal signs of high respect.
steps.whatToRemember: The elders answered every question wisely and stood firm against the king's power. In the end he honored them instead of punishing them.

phrases.english: Immediately he dressed them
in garments of purple,
and placed a chain of gold
on their necks.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The king's reaction to the elders' reply in step 35.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The king accepted the elders' answer and honored them.

steps.title: The king wants to go to אפריקי
steps.stepSummary: The king tells the elders he wants to go to the land of אפריקי, setting up a request for advice.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: I want to go to the country of אפריקי.
steps.whatsHappening: The story moves to a new subject. The king says he wants to travel to אפריקי, which sets up his request for the elders' advice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This line is a setup. By telling them his plan, the king is really asking what they think of it.

phrases.english: He said to them:
I want to go
to the country of Afriki.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהֹן: בָּעֵינָא דְּאֵיזִיל לִמְדִינַת אַפְרִיקֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new episode after the king honors the elders.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The elders' opinion about his journey to אפריקי.

steps.title: You can't go, because the Mountains of Darkness block the way
steps.stepSummary: The elders tell the king he cannot get there, because the Mountains of Darkness cut off the route.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: You cannot go, because the Mountains of Darkness block the way.
steps.whatsHappening: The elders warn the king that the trip is impossible. The Mountains of Darkness stand in the way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They do not argue about whether the war is a good idea. They point to a real obstacle on the road.

phrases.english: They said to him:
You are not able to go,
because the Mountains of Darkness block the way.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the king's plan in step 37.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The journey is impossible because the Mountains of Darkness block the route.

steps.title: I must go, so tell me how
steps.stepSummary: The king insists he must go, explains that this is exactly why he asked, and wants to know what to do.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: I have no choice but to go. That is exactly why I am asking you. So what should I do?
steps.whatsHappening: The king refuses to give up the trip. He asks the elders for a practical way to get past the Mountains of Darkness. The next step gives their answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The king changes his question. He is not asking whether he should go anymore. He is asking how to do it. The next step gives the elders' answer.

keyTerms.meaning: It is impossible not to, there is no choice but
Because of this, for this reason

steps.confusionAlert: The king is not asking again whether to go. He has already decided. He now wants a practical way around the obstacle.

phrases.english: He said to them:
It is not possible that I not go,
and it is for this reason that I am asking you,
so rather, what should I do?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לְהֹן: לָא סַגִּיא דְּלָא אָזֵילְנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Pushes back on the elders' warning in step 38 and asks for a practical solution.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the king can get past the Mountains of Darkness to reach אפריקי.

steps.title: The elders' advice: donkeys that see in the dark, and ropes for the way back
steps.stepSummary: The elders tell the king to bring Libyan donkeys that walk in darkness and to tie ropes at the entrance so he can return.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Bring Libyan donkeys that walk in the dark. And bring coils of rope and tie them on this side, so that when you come back you can hold onto them and return to your place.
steps.whatsHappening: The elders answer the king's question from the last step. They tell him how to cross the Mountains of Darkness and get back safely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their plan solves two problems. The donkeys can find the path in the dark going in. The rope tied at the entrance is a guide line he can follow to come back out.

phrases.english: They said to him:
Bring Libyan donkeys
that walk in the darkness.
And bring coils of rope,
and tie them on this side,
phrases.notes: They mean the near side of the mountains, right where he goes in.

phrases.english: so that when you come back (by the road),
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets and some don't.

phrases.english: you can take hold of them
and come back to your place.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the king's request for a way to reach אפריקי
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Use donkeys that walk in the dark, and tie ropes at the entrance to guide the way back.

steps.title: The king travels and reaches a town of women
steps.stepSummary: The king follows the advice, reaches a town where everyone is a woman, and wants to make war with them.
steps.simpleTranslation: He did this and went. He came to a certain town that was all women, and he wanted to make war with them.
steps.whatsHappening: The story moves forward. The king follows the elders' advice and arrives at a town of only women, where he wants to fight. This sets up the women's reply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The advice worked, and he crossed the mountains. A new scene opens with a strange town whose people are all women, and a new problem: he wants to attack them.

phrases.english: He did this, and went.
He came to a certain town
that was all women.
He wanted to wage battle against them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Carries out the advice and opens a new episode
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The king reaches a town of women and plans to attack it.

steps.title: The women show that fighting them is a lose-lose
steps.stepSummary: The women argue that if he kills them he is shamed, and if they kill him he is shamed even more.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: If you kill us, people will say: He killed women. If we kill you, people will say: The king whom women killed.
steps.whatsHappening: The women push back against the king's plan to attack. They show him that the war can only hurt his name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This works like a challenge with two sides. If he wins, he looks shameful for killing women. If he loses, he is mocked forever as the king killed by women. Either way the battle does him no good.

phrases.english: They said to him:
If you kill us,
people will say: He killed women.
If we kill you,
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording, meaning 'we kill'.

phrases.english: people will say: The king whom women killed.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי קָטְלַתְּ לַן, יֵאמְרוּ: נְשֵׁי קְטַל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the king's plan to make war
steps.kashyaTarget: The king's plan to fight the town of women
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both possible outcomes of the battle bring the king shame, so the war makes no sense for him.

steps.title: The king asks for bread and receives bread of gold
steps.stepSummary: Instead of fighting, the king asks for bread, and the women bring him golden bread on a golden table.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Bring me bread. They brought him bread of gold on a table of gold.
steps.whatsHappening: The king drops the battle and asks for bread. The women bring him bread made of gold. This sets up the next part of the story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His request shows he accepted their argument and gave up the war. The golden bread is a strange answer to a request for food, and it prepares the point the story will make next.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't stop here thinking the story is over. The golden bread is a setup, and the point comes in the next lines.

phrases.english: He said to them: Bring me bread.
They brought him bread of gold
on a table of gold.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The king accepts the women's argument and changes course
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The king asks for bread, and the women serve him bread of gold on a golden table, setting up the next exchange.
